meta.title: Hestia
meta.description: Finding unmapped villages and routing vaccination teams to them.

home.lead: Currently, over 1.9 billion people have no access to healthcare, just because of where they live.
home.mapLead: The global rural healthcare issue stems from 3 reasons: 1) Governments don't know where people live, 2) Governments don't know the most efficient way to reach them, and 3) Governments don't know how much it will cost to help. Each of these issues comes from a lack of data, data that we now provide through computer vision on satellites and OpenStreetMap information. Click into a country to see our scans along with all of their information.

problem.title: Problem
problem.subtitle: Globally, 1.9 billion people have no access to healthcare just because they live in rural regions of their country.
problem.locationBody1: Many offical maps used by governments in order to give data to health facilities are missing many rural villages. This is especially common in developing countries. Without the maps knowing where these people are, the only way to find them is using a satelite.
problem.locationBody2: This was explicitly proven in 2025, when a scientific study compared the five most popular population maps against real-life headcounts in rural areas of the world. None of them were anywhere near the corrent answer. Instead, they all heavily underestimated the region's full population. The best map, WorldPop, only accounted for 47% of the region's population.
problem.mapCaption: Offical maps often hide villages that we can find through satellite imagery
problem.undercountCaption: How much each population map undercounted rural residents, on average (1975–2010)
problem.routesTitle: Clinics don't know the cheapest way to reach them
problem.routesBody1: Even if the government knows where the villages are, they still don't always know the most efficient way to reach them.
problem.routesBody2: With a large majority of all health clinics being in cities or towns, it can be incredibly difficult to figure out which clinic should take the effort to reach the nearest villages.
problem.routesBody3: Along with the issue of which clinic should attempt to reach the village, there is also the issue of how they should plan to get there, as the shortest route is often not the cheapest. To solve something like this, the health clinic would need some way to consistently weigh different terrians across paths.
problem.travelCaption: Out of every 100 people in the world, how far each one is from the nearest health facility
problem.byCar: More than an hour away, even by car
problem.onFoot: Reachable by car, but more than an hour's walk
problem.routeCaption: The shortest route on the map isn't always the cheapest
problem.fundingTitle: Rural clinics don't get enough money
problem.fundingBody1: In order to split the money between different health facilities, the cost of travel and number of people visited must be known precisly. In the case of rural facilities, neither of these values are known(due to issues 1 and 2). Without them, governments do not know how much money to give each facility, which severly limits the amount of good they can do.
problem.fundingBody2: This is due to what happens when the government is not given a precise cost estimate. Without knowing the true cost of serving their people, governments worry about overspending and wasting resources that could be used elsewhere. As overspending becomes the main thought in their minds, the result is almost always underspending, which can lead to incredible plans going unfullfilled.
problem.chainCaption: How a missing village loses its funding
problem.chain1Text: Satellites can see the roofs, but the official map is empty.
problem.chain2Text: Population estimates leave the people out.
problem.chain3Text: Money is split by headcount, so none is set aside.
problem.chain4Text: The nearest clinic is short on staff, vaccines and fuel.
problem.costChainCaption: How a missing cost estimate leads to underspending
problem.cost1Text: Nobody knows what staff, fuel and travel to each village will cost.
problem.cost2Text: Planners have to guess how much rural outreach needs.
problem.cost3Text: Running out of money halfway through is risky, so they guess low.
problem.cost4Text: Trips get cut, and the farthest villages are dropped first.

diagrams.mapGapLabel: On the official map the area shows one road and one town with a clinic. The satellite view of the same area shows four more villages that the map leaves out.
diagrams.routeDiagramLabel: Three clinics could reach the settlement. The cheapest trip follows a paved road, then a dirt track, then a short stretch with no road.

solution.title: Solution
solution.subtitle: Finds settlements, a route, and cost.
solution.findTitle: Satellites find the roofs maps forgot
solution.findBody1: A study in 2025 showed that the best population maps in the world today still miss over half the population in the rural areas they cover. Instead, Hestia uses satllite imagery to identify settlements that those population maps missed.
solution.findBody2: Hestia uses Microsoft building outline data as a first pass over an area. Learn more about how they are grouped in the Algorithm page.
solution.findBody3: When Microsoft doesn't have data for a scan, Hestia downloads images from the Esri World Imagery Wayback, whose photos we run our custom algorithm over.
solution.step1Text: Microsoft outlines by default, but resorts to satellite without it.
solution.step2Text: Each building is drawn on a grid to remove everything but the homes.
solution.step3Text: Nearby buildings are combined into a settlement.
solution.step4Text: To display, we outline them to make them easy to see.
solution.factGapLabel: largest gap between buildings in one settlement
solution.factHomeLabel: people per home (average household in Nigeria)
solution.checkTitle: Most of Hestia's settlements haven't been mapped
solution.checkBody1: To be sure, Hestia compares its results with OpenStreetMap to check for neighboring homes, outputting a certainty score of 100.
solution.checkBody2: If OpenStreetMap doesn't return anything nearby we limit our certainty to 99 and use three signs of a settlement to build that value. Building count, compactness, and building cover (the amount of outline that looks like roof).
solution.matchCaption: The split of our scans by whether OpenStreetMap returns a nearby home.
solution.scoreCaption: Scoring a settlement OpenStreetMap doesn't know about (0-99)
solution.scoreCoverDetail: full points at 15% of the outline (35% roof pixels with the color backup)
solution.scoreFootnote: That adds up to {total} points. The score stops at 99, because only an OpenStreetMap match can reach 100.
solution.reachTitle: Finding the cheapest route from a clinic
solution.reachBody1: Through OpenStreetMap, Hestia finds different types of health facilities in a 40 km radius of the scan by default, but if nothing is found, the search area increases to 660 km. After finding a facility it builds a map of all the roads a vehicle can traverse (it skips this if no facility is found).
solution.reachBody2: Hestia finds the cost of a journey from the three closest health facilities found near each settlement and keeps the least expensive one. Different types of road have different costs.
solution.reachBody3: In addition to cost, each trip is allotted a difficulty score, keeping track of the terrain and time needed to make the expedition.
solution.routeCaption: Hestia tries the three nearest clinics and keeps the cheapest trip
solution.rateCaption: Travel cost per kilometer, by OpenStreetMap road type (US$)
solution.rateNote: Roads that are usually paved cost 1.5 times more if OpenStreetMap says they are dirt, gravel or sand. We chose these rates for planning. They have not been measured in the field yet.
solution.tourBody1: Plotting and following a route to each settlement means the health team would need to traverse the same road many, many times. To counteract this, Hestia plots a trip through all settlements (with high certainty scores) in a scan so the health team can minimize cost.
solution.tourBody2: The clinic route is replanned every time a new scan is saved to make sure it is as optimal as we can make it.
solution.diagramCaption: One team, one loop out of the clinic and back

algorithm.title: Algorithm
algorithm.subtitle: Seven steps. One groundbreaking algorithm.
algorithm.seeLines: See these lines in the code
algorithm.sourceLead: Here's the detector code every scan runs (commented) (detect-villages.js on the command line calls it). Open a step above to jump to that part, or download the whole file to use!
algorithm.scanSource: Every scan runs this file. Help us scan a region!
algorithm.pictureText: First we download the outline of every building in a small box of land from Microsoft's global building map.
algorithm.pictureDetail: Microsoft's global building map was built on an AI model trained with satellite imaging of the whole world. A scan is about 4 by 4 kilometers and we only keep the buildings whose center is inside the box.
algorithm.roofsTitle: Backup plan: find roofs by color
algorithm.roofsText: Some places Microsoft doesn't have any data for, so there we look for roofs in the satellite photos ourselves.
algorithm.roofsDetail: We exclude trees, water and shadows. Pale concrete and blue metal are always counted as a roof, while red, teal and flat gray only count if there's a sharp edge. Red soil, dirt roads and asphalt are the same colors and their edges fade out slowly, so they are also excluded.
algorithm.joinText: Buildings within about 50 meters of each other go into the same settlement, and then we create a mesh and then a polygon around the group.
algorithm.joinDetail: We draw every building onto a 3 meter grid, fill in the gaps between the ones that are close and trace around each group. One house by itself still counts as a settlement. If a group is only tiny sheds and granaries we drop it though, because nobody lives in those.
algorithm.checkTitle: Check if it's already on the map
algorithm.checkText: If OpenStreetMap has a village, hamlet, town, suburb or lone homestead inside the outline or within 150 meters of it, we call it an 100% match, even without a set name.
algorithm.checkDetail: When the map doesn't have anything there, we score the settlement out of 99: 45 points for how many buildings it has (full at 8), 30 for how compact it is and 25 for how much of it is buildings. Only places that are already on the map get 100. The code here is the color backup's version, where full marks for that last part means 35% of the outline looks like roof. With Microsoft's outlines the same weights are used further down the file, and full marks there is 15% of the outline covered by buildings.
algorithm.costText: We count population as 4.7 people per home(Nigeria's average), using the average number of people per home in the region. Vaccines are counted as $10 a person and the visit itself is another $100.
algorithm.costDetail: Anything under 10 square meters is probably a granary or shed, so we don't count it. A normal house is one home, and a really big building counts as one home for every 150 square meters. With the color backup we can't measure buildings, so we count 5 people per roof or 5 per 250 square meters of settlement, whichever is more, and never fewer than 5.
algorithm.tripTitle: Find a clinic and price the trip
algorithm.tripText: No matter what, we keep scanning nearby areas until we find a clinic. We then price the trips from the nearby clinics, checking the three closest clinics for the cheapest trip, not the closest.
algorithm.tripDetail: The search starts at about 40 kilometers and goes out bit by bit to about 660. If there's still no clinic that far out, the trip is priced as about 660 kilometers with no road and no clinic. Paved roads are generally the cheapest per kilometer, while tracks cost more and anywhere off-road costs the most. If the clinic is really far out, we prioritize using main roads for a majority of the drive.
algorithm.tourTitle: Plan one trip for the team
algorithm.tourText: One team leaves a clinic, stops at every settlement and comes back, in whatever order is cheapest. Each trip depends on the shared clinic, not just the region, giving us the best possible route for each trip.
algorithm.tourDetail: The trip starts at the most popularly scanned clinic. If there's no clinic, it starts at the settlement closest to a road. At first it just keeps going to the cheapest stop that's left. Then we check the trip by predicting the alternative route, if the loop was flipped, then pick the cheapest solution. Clinic trips are planned off other scans as well as it's own. Low certainty settlements are skipped(<30 certainty).

donate.title: Help get vaccines to villages that aren't on the map
donate.lead: A lot of rural villages just aren't on official maps, and if a village isn't on the map then nobody is going to plan a route there. So the people living there don't get vaccines. When you donate, it goes toward finding those villages and figuring out how to get to them.
donate.scanChoose: Can't donate right now? You can still help us scan a region.
donate.needLead: These are the real numbers on rural people, health coverage and kids who never got a vaccine.
donate.fact1Label: people live in rural areas, about 42% of the world's population.
donate.fact2Label: of rural people have no health coverage.
donate.fact3Label: rural people have no health coverage.
donate.fact4Label: babies got no vaccine in their first year of life in 2025.
donate.why1Title: Villages that aren't on the map get skipped
donate.why1Text: Health workers can only go where they know people live. If a village never made it onto the map, nobody is ever going to plan a vaccine route out there.
donate.why2Title: Most rural people have no coverage
donate.why2Text: The ILO found that 56% of rural people don't have any health coverage. Put that together with the World Bank's 3.46 billion rural people and you get about 1.9 billion.
donate.why3Title: A route tells the money where to go
donate.why3Text: Once a government can actually see a village, and how to get there from the closest clinic, it finally knows where its health budget should go.
donate.whereLead: You choose which government gets your gift. We use it to find rural villages in that country that the health maps left out, and then we plan vaccine routes to them.
donate.where1Text: We look through satellite images and map data for settlements the official health maps left out.
donate.where2Text: Hestia finds the closest clinic and works out the best way from there to the village.
donate.where3Text: Your gift pays for the vaccines and for the health workers who make the trip out.
donate.chooseLead: In these 25 countries a lot of rural people still can't get health care. We'd go with the first one since it has the most rural people on the list.

explain.accessScale: Distance from a road counts most, then trip length, then how much of the way is rough. 0–33 is easy, 34–66 moderate, 67–100 hard.
explain.accessNoClinic: {label} ({score}/100): no clinic was found nearby, so the whole trip counts as off-road.
explain.osmConfirm: High: this settlement is listed on OpenStreetMap.
explain.osmConfirmNote: A mapped place inside the outline, or within {meters} m of it, confirms it.
explain.confidenceFootprints: {level}: its buildings are mapped, but OpenStreetMap has no name for the place (score {score}/100).
explain.confidenceFootprintNote: More buildings, a compact shape and more of the outline covered by buildings all raise the score (full at 8 buildings, and at {coverage} covered). It stays below 100 unless OpenStreetMap names the place. High is 75+, Medium 50–74, Low under 50.
explain.confidenceColorNote: More roofs, a compact shape and more roof-colored ground all raise the score. It stays below 100 unless OpenStreetMap confirms the place. High is 75+, Medium 50–74, Low under 50.
